q: A contract says 'the entire agreement is contained in this writing.' A party later claims a prior oral promise adds a term. Under the parol evidence rule, what will a court likely do?
r: Exclude the earlier oral promise that contradicts the final writing
A complete written contract controls over prior talks.
w: Add the oral promise to the contract
The writing is meant to be final.
Require the parties to restart negotiations

q: What is anticipatory repudiation?
r: One party clearly states before performance is due that it will not perform
The other party may treat it as a breach.
w: Assigning the contract to someone else
That is not a clear refusal.

q: A builder tells a homeowner in March that she will not build the June project at all. What may the homeowner do?
r: Treat it as a breach now and seek another builder
Repudiation lets the other party act early.
w: Wait silently until June before doing anything
Sue for the builder's profits only
Do nothing because no breach occurred yet

q: What is substantial performance?
r: Performance that meets the essential purpose of a contract even with minor flaws
The other party must pay, less any damages.
w: Doing exactly what was promised in every detail

q: A painter finishes a house but misses one small closet wall. The owner refuses to pay. What does substantial performance generally allow?
r: Payment less the cost to fix the small defect
The main purpose was met.

q: What is an accord and satisfaction?
r: An agreement to accept a different performance in place of the original duty, then carrying it out
It settles a dispute.
w: A contract that is never signed

q: What is a novation?
r: Replacing a party or contract with a new one, with the consent of all involved
The original party is released.
w: A contract signed by one party only

q: A supplier and a buyer agree that a new company will take over the supplier's contract and the original supplier is released. What is this?
r: A novation
The original party is replaced and released.
w: The original party would remain liable.

q: What is the duty to mitigate damages?
r: The injured party must take reasonable steps to reduce its losses
Damages may be reduced if it does not.
w: The injured party must increase its losses
The breaching party must pay double
The court must reduce all claims

q: A landlord's tenant leaves early. The landlord leaves the apartment empty for a year without trying to rent it. What principle may limit recovery?
r: The duty to mitigate damages
The landlord should try to re-rent.

q: What is an unconscionable contract?
r: One so one-sided and unfair that a court may refuse to enforce it
It shocks the conscience.
w: A contract with a low price

q: What is a contract of adhesion?
r: A standard take-it-or-leave-it contract drafted by one party
Consumers often have no room to negotiate.
w: A contract signed by sticking notes

q: A phone company's service contract allows it to change any term at any time without notice. A court might find it:
r: Possibly unconscionable or unenforceable in parts
Extreme one-sidedness can be struck down.

q: What is a click-wrap agreement?
r: An online contract in which a user clicks 'I agree' to accept terms
Courts often enforce them.
w: A contract written on paper only
A contract made only by phone

q: What does the E-SIGN Act do?
r: Gives electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper in many cases
It supports online contracts.
w: Requires every contract to be notarized

q: A customer signs a service contract using a typed name and a tablet. Is it likely valid?
r: Yes, electronic signatures are generally valid under E-SIGN
Intent to sign is what matters.

q: What is the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing?
r: A duty not to act to destroy the other party's right to the benefits of the contract
It applies to performance.
w: A duty to sign a second contract

q: What is the 'mirror image rule'?
r: An acceptance must match the offer's terms exactly under common law
A change makes it a counteroffer.
w: An offer must be written in mirrors
A seller must copy the buyer's logo

q: Under UCC 2-207 between merchants, an acceptance with additional minor terms generally:
r: Can form a contract, with the additional terms treated as proposals
The UCC relaxes the mirror image rule.

q: What is a firm offer under the UCC?
r: A merchant's signed written offer to buy or sell goods that stays open without consideration for a stated time
It is irrevocable for up to three months.
w: An offer made by a minor

q: What is an option contract?
r: An agreement, supported by payment, to keep an offer open for a set time
The holder may accept later.
w: A contract to sell stock only

q: A buyer pays $500 for the right to buy a property for $200,000 within 60 days. The seller cannot sell to others during that time. What is this?
r: An option contract
Payment keeps the offer open.

q: When can an offer be revoked?
r: Generally at any time before acceptance, unless it is an option or firm offer
The offeror controls it.

q: When does silence generally operate as acceptance?
r: Rarely, such as when the parties have a prior course of dealing
Silence is usually not acceptance.

q: What is the perfect tender rule?
r: A buyer may reject goods that fail in any respect to conform to the contract
The UCC sets a strict standard for single deliveries.
w: A seller may deliver any goods
A buyer must accept all goods
A seller may never deliver late

q: A seller delivers 100 blue mugs when the contract specified 100 red mugs. Under the perfect tender rule, the buyer may:
r: Reject the nonconforming goods
The goods do not match the contract.
w: Force the seller to paint them
The seller is the contracting party.

q: What is the seller's right to cure under the UCC?
r: The chance to fix a defective delivery within the contract time
It limits sudden rejection.
w: A right to cancel the contract
A right to double the price

q: What is 'cover' as a buyer's remedy?
r: Buying substitute goods after the seller fails to deliver and recovering the extra cost
It limits losses.

q: A seller fails to deliver 200 units at $10 each. The buyer buys 200 substitutes at $13 each. What may the buyer recover as cover damages?
r: $3 extra per unit times 200 units.
w: That is the number of units.

q: What is revocation of acceptance?
r: A buyer's right to cancel acceptance when a substantial defect was hidden or could not reasonably be found
It must happen within a reasonable time.

q: What is a bill of lading?
r: A document issued by a carrier acknowledging receipt of goods and stating shipping terms
It is a document of title.

q: What is a warehouse receipt?
r: A document issued by a warehouse acknowledging stored goods
It is a document of title.
w: A receipt for a rent payment

q: A seller learns before delivery that a buyer is insolvent. What right may the seller have?
r: To stop delivery or demand cash
The UCC protects sellers from unpaid sales.

q: What does the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act regulate?
r: Written warranties on consumer products
It requires clear disclosure.

q: What is the difference between a 'full' and a 'limited' warranty under Magnuson-Moss?
r: A full warranty gives stronger remedies such as repair or replacement without charge, while a limited warranty offers less
Labels must be clear.
w: A full warranty lasts one day
A limited warranty has no terms

q: An advertisement calls a product 'guaranteed for life,' but the written warranty excludes most defects. What legal concern arises?
r: Misleading or deceptive advertising and warranty disclosure
The claim does not match the terms.

q: What does the CAN-SPAM Act require of commercial emails?
r: A clear way to opt out, accurate sender and subject information
Violations can be fined.
w: That emails be sent only at night

q: What does COPPA protect?
r: The online privacy of children under 13
Sites need parental consent for data collection.

q: A game app collects names and locations of 9-year-olds without parental consent. Which law is most likely violated?
r: COPPA
It governs children's data.

q: What is the Do Not Call Registry intended to do?
r: Let consumers limit unwanted telemarketing calls
Telemarketers must honor it.

q: What is the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's role?
r: Protects consumers in financial products and services
It enforces consumer finance laws.

q: Under federal law, a cardholder reports an unauthorized charge on a credit card within 60 days. What is the typical maximum liability?
r: The Fair Credit Billing Act caps liability.

q: Who is a holder in due course?
r: A person who takes a negotiable instrument for value, in good faith and without notice of defects
They get special protection.
w: A person who steals the instrument
A person who knows it is forged
A person who receives it as a gift

q: A buyer pays a seller with a note, and the seller sells the note to a bank that took it in good faith for value. The buyer claims the goods were defective. Against the bank, the buyer's defense is generally:
r: Limited, because the bank is a holder in due course
Personal defenses are cut off.
w: HDC status cuts off personal defenses.

q: What is a real defense against a holder in due course?
r: A defense that works even against a HDC, such as forgery or fraud in the factum
It goes to the validity of the instrument.

q: What is a stop-payment order?
r: A customer's instruction to a bank not to pay a particular check
It must be timely.
w: An order to close an account
An order to raise a limit
An order to print a statement

q: A customer writes a check, then learns the goods were not delivered. What can she do if the check has not yet cleared?
r: Place a stop-payment order with the bank
It can prevent payment.
w: Mail the check back to the store only
That is not a bank order.

q: What is a cashier's check?
r: A check drawn by a bank on its own funds
It is considered more secure.
w: A check written by a store clerk
A personal check on a closed account

q: What is a certified check?
r: A personal check the bank has guaranteed by setting aside the funds
The bank becomes primarily liable.
w: A check approved by a customer
A check with a certificate of origin

q: Which is generally safer for a seller receiving a large payment from an unknown buyer?
r: A cashier's check from a verified bank
The bank backs the payment.
w: That is not a valid instrument.

q: What is forgery in the context of checks?
r: Signing another person's name without authority
The forged signature is generally ineffective.

q: What does the Electronic Fund Transfer Act protect?
r: Consumers using electronic payments such as debit cards and ATMs
It limits liability for unauthorized transfers.

q: A consumer reports a lost debit card within two business days. Under the EFTA, her liability for unauthorized use is generally capped at:
r: Prompt reporting limits liability.
w: The cap is $50 for timely reports.

q: What is the business judgment rule?
r: Courts generally will not second-guess directors' good-faith, informed decisions
It protects reasonable business choices.
w: A rule that directors must always profit
A rule banning directors from risks

q: A board makes an informed, good-faith decision to enter a new market that loses money. Shareholders sue. Under the business judgment rule, the directors are likely:
r: Protected from liability
Poor results alone do not prove wrongdoing.

q: What is a derivative lawsuit?
r: A suit by a shareholder on behalf of the corporation against insiders or others who harmed it
Any recovery goes to the corporation.
w: A suit by employees for wages
A suit on a derivative stock

q: What is a proxy in corporate voting?
r: Authority given to another person to vote a shareholder's shares
It allows voting without attending.
w: A fee paid to attend meetings

q: What is cumulative voting?
r: A system letting shareholders concentrate their votes on fewer director candidates
It can help minority holders.
w: A system of one vote per director

q: A shareholder with 100 shares can elect 3 directors under cumulative voting. How many votes can she cast for one candidate?
r: 100 shares times 3 seats.
w: That is the number of seats.

q: What is a merger?
r: The combination of two corporations in which one survives
The other ceases to exist.
w: A split of one company into many

q: What is a hostile takeover?
r: An attempt to acquire a company against the wishes of its management
It may go directly to shareholders.

q: What is dissolution of a corporation?
r: The legal end of a corporation's existence
Assets are liquidated and debts paid.

q: On dissolution, who is generally paid first from a corporation's assets?
r: Creditors
Shareholders receive what remains.

q: What is a registered agent?
r: A person or company designated to receive legal documents for a business
States require one.

q: What is a DBA ('doing business as') filing?
r: Registering a trade name different from the owner's legal name
It informs the public who owns the business.

q: Maria runs 'Sunrise Landscaping' as a sole proprietor. What may she be required to file?
r: A DBA or fictitious business name registration
Local rules often require it.

q: What is a benefit corporation?
r: A corporation that commits to public benefit goals in addition to profit
It balances purpose and profit.
w: A corporation that pays no taxes

q: What is a cooperative?
r: A business owned and controlled by its members who use its services
Profits are shared among members.
w: A business owned by one person
A business owned by the government

q: What duties does an agent owe a principal?
r: Loyalty, obedience, care and accounting
Agents must act in the principal's interest.
w: Only the duty to be paid

q: A real estate agent secretly buys a property she was hired to find for a client at a lower price and resells it to the client at a markup. What duty is violated?
r: Loyalty
The agent put her own interest first.

q: What duties does a principal owe an agent?
r: Compensation, reimbursement and a safe working environment
Principals must treat agents fairly.
w: A duty to sell the business

q: What is an undisclosed principal?
r: A principal whose existence is unknown to the third party dealing with the agent
The principal may still be bound.
w: A principal who cannot be sued

q: How can an agency relationship be terminated?
r: By agreement, completion of the task, revocation or the death of a party
Several events end it.

q: A principal tells an agent to stop acting for her, but the agent still signs a contract with a vendor who had dealt with him before and was not told. The principal may still be bound by:
r: Lingering apparent authority
Third parties must be notified of termination.
w: Nothing, because notice is never needed

q: What is the 'scope of employment'?
r: The range of activities an employee is hired or authorized to perform
Employers are liable for acts within it.

q: An employee takes a personal day trip in a company car and causes a crash. Is the employer likely liable?
r: Probably not, if the trip was outside the scope of employment
A personal frolic differs from work.
w: Liable only if the car is red

q: What is a joint employer?
r: Two or more businesses that share control over a worker's terms
Both may be responsible under labor laws.
w: A worker who has two names

q: What does the 'ABC test' do in some states?
r: Helps decide whether a worker is an employee or independent contractor
It presumes employee status unless conditions are met.

q: What is a security deposit in a lease?
r: Money paid by a tenant to cover potential damage or unpaid rent
It is generally refundable minus lawful deductions.

q: A landlord keeps a tenant's entire deposit to cover normal wear and tear such as faded paint. This is generally:
r: Not allowed in most places
Normal wear and tear is not deductible.

q: What is the implied warranty of habitability?
r: A landlord's duty to keep rental housing safe and livable
It covers basics like heat and plumbing.
w: A landlord's duty to buy furniture

q: What is eviction?
r: The legal process of removing a tenant from rental property
It requires following legal steps.

q: A landlord changes the locks while a tenant is at work, with no court order. This is generally called:
r: An illegal self-help eviction
Landlords must use legal process.

q: What is a deed?
r: A legal document that transfers ownership of real property
It is signed and delivered.

q: What is a quitclaim deed?
r: A deed that transfers whatever interest the grantor has, without warranties
It offers little protection to the buyer.
w: A deed that guarantees clear title
A deed that cancels a mortgage
A deed that sells a car

q: A buyer wants the strongest protection about clear ownership. Which deed should she prefer?
r: A general warranty deed
The seller guarantees clear title.

q: What is title insurance?
r: Insurance protecting a buyer or lender against defects in a property's title
It covers past hidden claims.

q: What is zoning?
r: Local rules controlling how land can be used
Examples include residential and commercial zones.

q: A business wants to open a loud factory in a residential zone. What may it need?
r: A zoning variance or rezoning approval
Use must match zoning rules.
w: Nothing, because it is private land

q: What is an easement?
r: A right to use another person's land for a limited purpose
A utility line is an example.

q: What is adverse possession?
r: Gaining title to land by openly occupying it for a statutory period
The occupation must meet strict conditions.

q: What is comparative negligence?
r: A rule that reduces damages by the plaintiff's share of fault
Fault is divided.

q: A jury finds a plaintiff 30% at fault and awards $50,000 total damages. Under comparative negligence, what does she recover?
r: $50,000 reduced by 30%.
w: That is her share of fault.

q: What is assumption of risk?
r: A defense when a plaintiff knowingly accepted the danger that caused the injury
It can bar or reduce recovery.

q: What is premises liability?
r: A property owner's responsibility for injuries caused by unsafe conditions
Duty depends on the visitor's status.

q: A customer is injured by a broken stair in a store that knew about it for weeks. The store's likely exposure is:
r: Liability for failing to repair or warn
Known hazards must be addressed.
w: No liability because customers should look

q: What is a nuisance in tort law?
r: An unreasonable interference with another's use and enjoyment of land
Noise or smells can qualify.

q: What is trespass?
r: Unauthorized entry onto another's land
Intent to enter is enough.

q: What is tortious interference with contract?
r: Intentionally causing someone to breach a contract with another
It is an intentional tort.

q: A competitor secretly offers a supplier a bribe to break its contract with a rival. Which tort is most likely?
r: Tortious interference with contract
It induces a breach.

q: What is a patent's three main types in the U.S.?
r: Utility, design and plant
Each protects a different kind of invention.

q: What does a design patent protect?
r: The ornamental appearance of an item
It lasts 15 years from grant.

q: A company invents a new chair shape that looks distinctive. Which protection best covers its appearance?
r: A design patent
It protects ornamental design.

q: How long does copyright generally last for a work created by an individual today?
r: The author's life plus 70 years
Terms differ for works made for hire.

q: What does the DMCA do?
r: Provides a process for removing infringing online content and limits liability for platforms that comply
It addresses digital copyright.

q: What is trade dress?
r: The overall look and feel of a product or its packaging that identifies its source
It can be protected like a trademark.

q: A knockoff restaurant copies the exact decor, uniforms and layout of a famous chain, causing customer confusion. Which claim might apply?
r: Trade dress infringement
The overall look identifies the brand.

q: What is a domain name dispute often called when someone registers a famous brand's name to profit?
r: Cybersquatting
Federal law addresses it.

q: What is diversity jurisdiction?
r: Federal court authority over disputes between citizens of different states with enough money at stake
It is one basis for federal jurisdiction.

q: A citizen of Ohio sues a citizen of Texas for $200,000 over a contract. Which court may have jurisdiction beyond state court?
r: A federal district court under diversity jurisdiction
Different states and enough in controversy.
w: The Supreme Court as first instance

q: What is venue?
r: The proper geographic location for a trial
It is usually where parties live or events occurred.

q: What is a motion to dismiss?
r: A request that the court end a case because the claim is legally insufficient
It is made early.
w: A request for a bigger jury
A request to change the judge's name

q: Both parties agree on all facts and ask the judge to decide who wins as a matter of law. Which motion fits?
r: Summary judgment
It avoids a trial when no facts are disputed.

q: What is a verdict?
r: The decision of a jury on the facts of a case
A judge issues a judgment.

q: What does an appellate court generally review?
r: Whether legal errors occurred in the lower court
It usually does not retry the facts.

q: What is a default judgment?
r: A judgment for the plaintiff when the defendant fails to respond
It follows failure to answer.
w: A judgment for the defendant when the plaintiff dies

q: A business is served with a lawsuit and ignores it for months. What may happen?
r: The court may enter a default judgment against it
Ignoring a lawsuit has serious consequences.

q: What is a settlement?
r: An agreement between parties to resolve a dispute without a trial
It often involves payment.

q: What is garnishment of wages?
r: A court-ordered withholding of part of pay to satisfy a debt
Limits protect basic income.

q: After winning a money judgment, how may a creditor collect from a debtor who refuses to pay?
r: Through legal remedies such as wage garnishment or levies
Courts provide enforcement tools.

q: A company's code of ethics bans gifts over $50, but a vendor offers a manager tickets worth $400. What should the manager do?
r: Decline or report the offer according to policy
It violates the gift policy.
w: Accept and give a better deal to the vendor

q: What is 'tone at the top'?
r: Leaders' behavior and messages that set the ethical culture of an organization
Employees follow what leaders do.

q: What is ethical relativism?
r: The view that ethics depend on cultural or personal standards
It denies a single universal standard.
w: The view that laws never change
The belief in one set of rules everywhere

q: A firm abroad is told local custom accepts small bribes to speed permits. A U.S. company is bound by which law?
r: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act
U.S. companies cannot bribe foreign officials.

q: What is utilitarianism in ethics?
r: Choosing the action that creates the greatest good for the greatest number
It focuses on consequences.

q: What is deontological ethics?
r: Judging actions by whether they follow moral duties or rules
It focuses on duty.

q: A manager reasons, 'I should never lie, even if lying would help the company.' Which ethical approach is this?
r: Duty-based (deontological)
It emphasizes rules and duties.

q: What is insider information in ethics?
r: Confidential knowledge not available to the public that could influence decisions
Using it unfairly can be illegal.

q: What is an ethics audit?
r: A review of how well an organization follows its ethical policies
It finds gaps.

q: After an ethics audit finds repeated gift-policy violations, what is the best response?
r: Retrain staff, enforce the policy and fix incentives
It addresses root causes.

q: What is greenwashing?
r: Making misleading claims that a product or company is environmentally friendly
It deceives consumers.
